title: Loading for the Job - What to Bring

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Shop warehouse aisle with shelves of connectors, ladders on a rack, recycle containers stacked. A tech with a clipboard holding the project specifics sheet and survey. Danny, medium shot.
scenes.on_screen: Job Mindset: Load Without Being Told
scenes.says: A forgotten box of disconnects, a missing ladder or a vehicle that's too small means a trip back to the shop or a crew standing around on night one. Loads also shift and hurt people. So plan the load from the paperwork two days out, work out the worst case on quantities, strap everything, and call about shortages while there's still time to fix them.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: The tech reads the survey: two 12 ft ladders, a scissor lift, lots of old fixtures coming back. She calls her supervisor on the phone.
scenes.on_screen: Project size | Job type | Project specifics
scenes.says: Three things tell you what to bring: the project size, the job type and the project specifics. Watch her. Two days before a medium-size change-out, she sees two 12-foot ladders, a scissor lift and a lot of old fixtures coming back. Old fixtures often take more room than new material. So she calls her supervisor now to arrange a trailer, not on load day.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Items laid out in a row on the shop floor as they're named: ladders, connectors, rags, drop cloths, vacuum, cart, trash cans, tape gun, recycle containers, marker, shrink wrap, cones and caution tape, tablet.
scenes.says: Build the load in layers. First the core kit for every project: 6 and 8-foot ladders, wire nuts and lever-nut connectors or in-line disconnects, rags, drop cloths, a vacuum, a cart, trash cans with wheels, bags, tape gun, recycle containers, a marker, shrink wrap, cones and caution tape, and a tablet with recaps and timecards. Plus a drill, bits, meter and lockout kit for every person.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Close-up: the tech reads the capacity label on a recycle container, then writes on the back of the sheet: '720 lamps / 50 per container = 14.4, load 15'.
scenes.says: Work quantities out from the survey, not from the last job. Recycle containers: check how many lamps that container holds, then divide and round up. Write your working on the sheet, like 720 lamps divided by 50 is 14.4, load 15. Disconnects: one per fixture where the sheet calls for them, plus spares. More spares on an out-of-town run.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: The tech counts disconnects off the shelf and finds it short; she calls her supervisor from the shop aisle.
scenes.on_screen: Report shortages BEFORE you leave the shop
scenes.says: She counts disconnects off the shelf, and it's short. She calls her supervisor before she leaves, not after. That's when it can still be ordered or sent. Check items off as they go on the vehicle, not from memory. Ask before substituting a connector, ladder or fastener. And count expensive material when loading and again on site.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Ladders strapped on the rack, long cartons strapped in the trailer, scissor lift chained and bound; the tech checks the hitch, ball lock and chains.
scenes.on_screen: Safety: Strap ladders and cartons. Chain and bind the lift.
scenes.says: Safety equipment is on the list too: cones, caution tape, binders, chains and ratchet straps. A full vehicle is heavy and loads shift. Ladders and long cartons get strapped, and lifts get chained and bound on the trailer. Check the hitch, ball lock and chains. Never leave a lift or ladder unsecured to save time.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny at a ceiling grid mock-up pointing at seismic tie wires and MC cable supported off the tile.
scenes.on_screen: Support new wiring off the tile | Seismic ties per specifics and local code
scenes.says: Watch for job specifics. When new power is run, support the MC cable so it doesn't lie on the ceiling tile, and bring the right clips. Lay-in fixtures require seismic ties, a company rule, and the details depend on the local building code and seismic area, so follow the project specifics and your supervisor. Bring retrofit parts only when the specifics call for them.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Last night of the job: old tubes going into new-kit boxes, both ends taped, labeled 'OLD/USED LAMPS FOR RECYCLE'; the pallet shrink-wrapped and photographed; the tech noting it on the ticket.
scenes.on_screen: OLD/USED LAMPS FOR RECYCLE | Tape both ends | Shrink-wrap | Photograph | Note it on the ticket
scenes.says: Cut to the last night. Old tubes go into the new boxes, both ends taped, no lamps showing, labeled Old Used Lamps for Recycle. Keep recycle together, never mixed with good material, and ask before starting a new pallet. Shrink-wrap it, note it on the ticket, and always photograph it. We've been blamed for poor palletizing before. Your photo is the proof. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Shop load-out two days before a medium-size fixture change-out, then the last night of the job. Quantities shown are the lesson's example figures; label them as examples on screen. Recycle container capacity must match the container actually filmed. Seismic tie shot is a mock-up; do not imply one method fits every jurisdiction.
